doc.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06

title: Outside influences in New Orleans and Jay Cave on bass
summary: Huntington argues outsiders enrich the city, and says bassist Jay Cave, brought by Burton, taught him upright bass.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: But another thing he did. And this goes back to it's very important in New Orleans to have outside influences because what happens, like in the case of Maus, you get these outside influences, they come to the city, Bill Evans is another example, they develop. And they develop, it's a give and take, it's a compromise with the city. They absorb things from the city and the city absorbs things from them. And I think that connection is really important. Anyway, it's kind of New York in a way. It's kind of what's been happening all, you know, somebody, Ellis once said to me, nobody's from New York. You know, it's like New Yorkers are all from somewhere else. You know, in a sense, a lot of the New Orleans scene has been that way too. And a lot of the greatest New Orleans musicians are people who developed here who came from somewhere else, like in the case of Maus and Bill Evans, you know. But, so, oh, talking about Joe Burton, anyway, he comes and he has this gig and he has this club on Canal Street and Jeff Davis. Very nice club. And the thing that he did was bring Jay Cave to town. Jay Cave was a bass player from Philly who had played with Nita Simone, John Erdly, Benny Goodman. He had a lot of experience, excellent musician, excellent bass player, kind of in a Doug Watkins, early Ray Brown mode. Came to town and I, that's my first real introduction other than hearing Chuck Beatty. I hadn't really heard Richie play that much other than hearing Chuck Beatty play at the jazz room, Dominic's jazz room, which is one of those beatnik hangouts we're talking about with Ed Blackwell. Other than hearing Chuck Beatty, I hadn't really heard this kind of bass playing until I heard Jay. And then sitting next to Jay every night and playing like,

four or five hour gig with him was really an education and really taught me more about bass than anybody I studied with. And that's when I really became interested in playing upright bass and that's when I switched over right around that time. And then started all the things that happened at the Playboy Club, started playing with Buddy Prima and so on, again on bass at this time,
So by that time, Charlie, I think you were out of town, weren't you?
